A megtakarított energiamennyiségről megbízható adat csak később lesz elérhető. A paksi atomerőmű aktuális visszaterhelési értéke: 1770 megawatt, így az erőmű 2000 megawatt helyett 230 megawatton termel. A Balaton átlag vízállása 54 cm volt, ez az elmúlt napon nem változott. A Velencei-tó vízállása 28 cm, ez 1 centit csökkent. A Velencei-tó vízállása 24 cm-rel van a valaha mért legkisebb vízállás szintje alatt. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-buildings-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ikq4 Police cordons are set to remain for the time being Image: Felix Kirberg/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Buildings near a train station in the southern state of Bavaria were evacuated as a precaution on Thursday after police said that an object found on the tracks could contain explosives. Investigators later determined that the object was not an explosive, although criminal police were continuing work at the scene. A technician had discovered the suspicious item in the track bed at the entrance to the station in the town of Treuchtlingen. Specialists X-rayed the object, which was also lifted using a robot to allow further investigations. A federal police bomb disposal team is examining the object Image: Felix Kirberg/dpa/picture alliance Road and rail closures remain in place while the investigation continues. Regional services are affected, with trains terminating early at suitable stations. Replacement buses and large-capacity taxis have been arranged. Long-distance services are being diverted via the city of Ingolstadt. Police have urged people to avoid the area and take alternative routes. https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: A bluefin tuna was caught off the Yorkshire coast since 1960s after overfishing and the depletion of herring shoals had rendered the giant fish almost extinct in the North Sea. Photograph: 54 North Maritime training View image in fullscreen A bluefin tuna was caught off the Yorkshire coast since 1960s after overfishing and the depletion of herring shoals had rendered the giant fish almost extinct in the North Sea. Photograph: 54 North Maritime training Fish First bluefin tunas caught off Yorkshire since 1960s ‘success story’ for marine conservation Researchers laud return of giant tuna to North Sea after being fished almost to point of extinction Raphael Boyd Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.36 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 13.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Researchers have lauded two giant bluefin tunas being caught off the coast of Yorkshire for the first time in more than six decades as a “success story” for marine conservation. The tunas, which were caught a day apart off the coast of Whitby earlier this week, have mostly been absent along the north-east coast of Britain since the 1960s. While small numbers of the species have been spotted in the waters around Yorkshire in the previous years, the pair were the first to be caught for market from the North Sea since licences to catch the fish were issued in July. Rodney Forster, a professor at the University of Hull and head of the Hull marine laboratory, called the tuna’s reappearance a “success story about the management of fisheries” in Britain. “They were fished almost to the point of extinction in their spawning grounds in the Mediterranean through the 70s and 80s,” said Forster. “But now careful protection of the stock means they’ve increased, even to the point that they’re now spreading back out to their old grounds around the UK and even into the Baltic Sea.” View image in fullscreen Trainee Ada Peake, 18, was part of the landing of the giant bluefin tuna. Photograph: 54 North Maritime training Forster said the tuna were not the only marine life that had returned to the Yorkshire coast, pointing out that minke whales and bottlenose dolphins had seen a noticeable increase in numbers around the North Sea over the past decade. Bryce Stewart, a senior research fellow at the Marine Biological Association, a marine charity based in Plymouth, called the return of bluefin tuna to the UK “fantastic” and lauded the work done by the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (Iccat) to re-establish populations. “It seemed like an era that had gone for ever, you know, I mean normally if we lose a large species like this from an area of sea, they don’t come back,” said Stewart. “So, as I said, both from a personal scientific point of view, this is a really wonderful thing to see.” Despite joy at the tuna population increasing around Yorkshire and beyond, concerns have also been raised that their increased numbers farther north could in part be linked to the effects of climate change. Both Forster and Stewart mentioned rising temperatures in the North Sea as another factor in the tuna’s return, albeit a less influential one than the management of fisheries. Stewart said the warmer temperatures had a “sort of knock-on effect” as the small fish that tuna eat, such as herring and sprat, do better in warmer temperatures. Both of the fish caught in Whitby were notably well fed, with each weighing about 320kg (700lb), roughly double the size of the average tuna found on the south coast. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion Climate change is one of many factors alongside pollution and illegal fishing that could prevent the tuna from properly re-establishing themselves along the Yorkshire coast, but there are hopes that if properly managed they can thrive there and even move into Scottish waters. Calum Duncan, the principal policy specialist at the Marine Conservation Society, lauded the regeneration of the tuna populations, but warned that their continued survival hinged on consistent care and for British fishing policies to place a greater onus on protecting marine ecology. “We’ve got a long, long way to go, but it’s really encouraging to have achieved this,” said Duncan. “Stories like the return of bluefin tuna send a clear signal that human beings can manage our way out of environmental decline by making good decisions and working together, making good plans and – most importantly – implementing them. But we just need to do a lot more of it and need to ramp it up.” Explore more on these topics Fish Marine life Wildlife Fishing industry Fishing Yorkshire England news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Fisher with a mission: first woman to chair Grayling Society wants to protect ‘lady of the stream’ Iberian orca known for ramming boats seen with suspected gunshot wounds UK waters hit with extreme heatwave as global sea temperatures reach record levels Hundreds of dead sharks and fish wash up on two beaches in Wales High levels of toxic ‘forever chemicals’ found off coast of southern England The rise of blue-space therapy: how the sea is helping people deal with trauma, anxiety and addiction Fish farms and pollution in Scotland Ocean surface temperatures hit a record high for June Cocaine pollution in rivers and lakes may disrupt behaviour of salmon, study finds Tiny Antarctic sea creature could be key to treating melanoma, researchers say Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

https://nineoclock.ro/radr2026-annual-me.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount #RADR2026: Annual Meeting of Romanian Diplomacy, Organized by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Bucharest on August 31 – September 1 29 August 2026 / By Mihai Manea , Publisher of N ine O’Clock Nine O’Clock received from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, at the newspaper’s editorial office, information regarding the organization of the 2026 Annual Meeting of Romanian Diplomacy (#RADR2026), which will take place in Bucharest between August 31 and September 1. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs will organize the Annual Meeting of Romanian Diplomacy (#RADR2026) on August 31 – September 1, 2026, one of the most important events dedicated to Romanian diplomacy. The meeting will take place at the Bucharest National Opera and will be chaired by Minister of Foreign Affairs Oana Țoiu. Held traditionally around Romanian Diplomacy Day, celebrated annually on September 1, the event will bring together the heads of Romania’s diplomatic missions and consular offices abroad, representatives of the foreign diplomatic corps accredited in Bucharest, members of the leadership of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as senior Romanian officials. Bahrain’s Foreign Minister, Special Guest The special guest of this year’s meeting is the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Bahrain, Abdullatif bin Rashid Al-Zayani. The participation of the Bahraini official highlights the international dimension of the meeting and Romania’s interest in strengthening relations with partners in the Gulf region. A More Efficient and Pragmatic Diplomacy This year’s edition of the Annual Meeting of Romanian Diplomacy is dedicated to a more efficient, pragmatic and better-connected diplomacy focused on Romania’s interests. Discussions will focus on how diplomatic and consular action can contribute more effectively to strengthening Romania’s international profile and promoting the country’s strategic interests. Key priorities include advancing Romania’s security and economic interests, supporting Romanian citizens at home and abroad, and strengthening Romania’s role within the European Union and in the transatlantic relationship. The meeting will also address the importance of developing Romania’s dialogue with global partners and adapting diplomatic action to an international environment that is undergoing continuous change. Through the meeting, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs aims to strengthen coordination between the ministry’s central structure and Romania’s diplomatic and consular missions abroad, while establishing priorities and directions for the country’s foreign policy for the period ahead. The Annual Meeting of Romanian Diplomacy is held every year around September 1, Romanian Diplomacy Day, and represents an important opportunity to assess developments and establish the priorities of Romanian diplomacy. mihai.manea@nineoclock.ro (Photo source: www.mae.ro) The diplomatic daily newspaper Nine O’Clock does not assume responsibility for the information received and published on the public website. Beállítom Iváncsa önkormányzata vizsgálatot végeztetett a település kútjait érintően, miután kiderült, hogy NMP ipari oldószer került a talajba az iváncsai akkumulátorgyár területén. A most közzétett vizsgálati adatokból kiderül, hogy a kutak egyikében sem mutatható ki a magzatkárosító vegyi anyag jelenléte – írja az MTI. A település 55 helyszínén az elmúlt napokban fúrt és ásott kutakból vettek mintákat, amelyeket megvizsgálva kijelenthető, hogy az egyikben sem mutatható ki szennyeződés. A falu területén működő SK On Hungary akkumulátorgyár közölte, hogy az üzem belső területén található monitoring kútban mutatott ki NMP-szennyezést a gyár saját mérése. Az önkormányzat közölte, hogy a kontrollvizsgálatokat a továbbiakban is folytatni fogják. A Fejér vármegyei község múlt hét pénteken közölte, hogy a gyár NMP-szennyezést (n-metil-2-pirrolidon) fedezett fel. Már akkor közölték, hogy a vezetékes ivóvíz Ercsi felől érkezik csővezetéken, azzal nem lehet probléma. A szennyezést az SK On Hungary is megerősítette az MTI-nek, és azt írták: a vállalati eljárásaiknak megfelelően azonnal meghozták a szükséges óvintézkedéseket, például a vonatkozó berendezések üzemeltetésének felfüggesztését. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: A sign reading ‘Education in peril – angry youth’ on the gates of the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars in Sevran. Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A sign reading ‘Education in peril – angry youth’ on the gates of the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars in Sevran. Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian France ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state Students say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continue Angelique Chrisafis in Sevran Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O n a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-income banlieue town in the suburbs north-east of Paris. “There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.” The 17-year-old in his last year of high school wants to study management and digital communication at a Paris university. But he said conditions were so poor, he felt all odds were stacked against him and his classmates. “Some of us have to go months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced,” he said. “One class had no French teacher for several months just before the French baccalaureate, so they couldn’t even study all the set texts for their exam. Recently we needed a teacher for a subject taught through English, but when that teacher arrived they didn’t speak English.” The biggest youth protest movement in the country in decades brought hundreds of thousands on to the streets across France this week demonstrating against inequality in the French education system , decrepit schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes. Hundreds of schools were blockaded, thousands of teenagers were arrested, and rights groups warned of alleged police brutality , with one child losing the use of eye and another losing a hand. View image in fullscreen Graffiti on a wall at the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars. Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian Mohammed and his classmates, often supported by their parents and teachers, have been at the frontline, barricading their school, the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, which is in one of mainland France’s poorest départements , Seine-Saint-Denis. They have voted to continue their protests next week, taking their grievances to the local mayor, elected officials and education representatives. Many local politicians have supported their demands. Even the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, conceded that teenagers had “legitimate” concerns. Photos on the Sevran students’ phones showed broken classroom chairs, holes in walls, holes in ceilings, mould, buckets to catch leaks, faulty lights. They said basic needs weren’t met, with some toilets broken, others with no doors and often no toilet paper or soap. Video projectors and science equipment were lacking. View image in fullscreen A student shows an example of conditions in the school on their phone. Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian “We’re not asking for luxury, just the basics to learn in decent conditions,” Mohammed said. “And yet police on horseback charged us when we were gathered to protest outside our school, firing teargas at us and making arrests. It’s so dangerous to be charged by a horse, it could kill you. I just ran, I was trying to help my classmates.” The high schools of Seine-Saint-Denis, a suburban area nudging against northern Paris, have been a driving force in the protests. The area has the youngest population in mainland France , one of the highest birthrates and the among the lowest average income. Local high schools have a high turnover of young teachers. Despite co-hosting the 2024 Paris Olympics , and numerous government plans to try to combat long-running problems of inequality and poverty, the area north-east of Paris is still disadvantaged compared with the capital. In 2005, Seine-Saint-Denis was the starting point for weeks of unrest on housing estates across France, leading to a state of national emergency being declared, after the death of two young boys hiding from police in an electricity substation. This week’s protests have shown that inequality and discrimination has not been addressed in the Paris suburbs and the mistrust between young people and police persists. Sevran’s Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, with more than 1,000 pupils, has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before. In 2024, students and teachers made a viral video about the state of classrooms, toilets and equipment. The local Île de France region said it had put in place a major refurbishment project for high school buildings. But the teenagers said key issues had not been addressed. View image in fullscreen Lycée Blaise-Cendrars has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before. Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian “We’re starting at an unfair advantage because our parents aren’t as rich as others, they can’t buy us books, they can’t take us to films,” said Ilian, 17, whose family has Moroccan roots and whose father is a traffic warden. “We’re missing school during these protests, we risk falling behind in an exam year, we’re desperate to get back into class to study, but the conditions we’re facing are so bad we can’t stop until the government promises action.” The education ministry this week promised 3,000 teachers to urgently fill gaps, but teachers’ unions expressed doubts and said longer-term plans and more funding was needed, even if the government argues there is little spare cash. Children’s mental health is also an issue in Seine-Saint-Denis. Ilian has been waiting to see a child psychiatrist for months. At the high school, there was no school nurse and a lack of support staff for children with disabilities, he said. “The police look down on us as if we’re animals”, Ilian said. “They talk to us with such cruelty.” He told local politicians that some teenagers alleged police had made racial insults against them during protests. Stéphane Troussel, the Socialist head of the Seine-Saint-Denis département council who met the pupils this week, said: “It’s intolerable that policing is causing part of the difficulties.” He called for the police to stop using a type of rubber-bullet launcher, after they suspended use of stun grenades following injuries. The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has defended policing tactics. View image in fullscreen Stéphane Blanchet, the local mayor, meets students at the town hall. Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian Stéphane Blanchet, the mayor of Sevran, said he supported the school protesters’ demands. He said many in his town of 52,000 people, with a higher than average poverty rate, felt “relegated” and forgotten by the state. Sarah, 17, who wanted to study at an elite Paris engineering faculty, and whose warehouse worker father was proud she was protesting and meeting the mayor, said teenagers in the banlieue “really feel abandoned”. She said: “We’ve been surprised and so appreciative of other teenagers in better-off places in France marching in the streets to support us this week. We know we’re disadvantaged and that we have to work 10 times as hard as others to escape discrimination against our postcode. But we can’t learn properly in these conditions when we’re not even guaranteed a chair to sit on in school.” Students’ names have been changed Explore more on these topics France Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
